newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia-Japan coal talks on in tight market.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia-Japan coal talks on in tight market.

text.p: First formal negotiations on terms for Australian hard coking coal exports to Japan in 1997/98 open in Tokyo on Thursday, a spokesman for The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP) said on Wednesday.
The negotiations with Japanese steel mills led by Nippon Steel Corp, will fire opening shots in often-protracted talks to set prices and volumes for the Japanese fiscal year which begins on April 1.
Opening talks this year were expected to last a few days assuming there is no early settlement, BHP Australia Coal public affairs manager Ian Dymock said.

The negotiations are being conducted this year in an atmosphere of tight supply and are expected to lead to another price increase to follow the approximately six percent rise to about US$54.50 a tonne for hard coking coal set last year.

Another Australian coal executive, who asked not to be named, said representatives of most of the Western World's major hard coking coal producers, from Australia, Canada and the U.S., were in Tokyo this week or scheduled to fly in next week.
The supply/demand position on the three main types of coal --- hard coking, semi-soft and thermal --- varied between categories somewhat this year, he said.
Hard coking coal was in the tightest position and thermal in a relatively easy position, he said.
"That would lead me to believe that the price rise for hard coking will be bigger than for thermal, and semi-soft fits somewhere in between," he said.
This executive is privately forecasting slightly lower price increases for 1997/98 than achieved for the current year.

"Last year I forecast US$3.00, $2.00 and $1.00 (price increases per tonne for hard coking, semi-soft and thermal coals). That wasn't very far from the truth for the first two, although (the price) was rolled over for thermal," he said.
(BHP's hard coking coal price rose by about $3.50 a tonne.)
"This year my thinking is (for rises of) $2.00, $1.00 and zero, less than last year," he said.
Supply in semi-soft and thermal coals was slightly easier than last year, he said.

This early prediction falls far short of an opening informal shot fired by Australian hard coking coal producers after the Australia-Japan Business Cooperation Committee meetings in Sydney in October, when a hard coking coal price rise request of $6.00 a tonne, or more than 10 percent, was put before the Japanese.
This week's talks will be followed next week by opening negotiations on semi-soft coal pricing terms.
"I don't think anything of substance will come out in this first round," one Australian producer said.
The annual Australia-Japan coal pricing round is the most important determinant of coal prices in the Asian region and beyond.
Australian coal exports, which mostly go to Japan, are forecast to reach almost 150 million tonnes worth about A$8.2 billion in 1996/97 ending June 30.
